f3d6dd80c7563f6b949b.text: As you can see, some of these questions might be asked defiantly,

096dabc17770f7ebb1de.text: sarcastically, or even just to draw attention to certain facts. In each case, however, an answer is usually not expected.

dc0f398288423a7f4b2a.text: - are basically a requirement for any effective speech, which is why you’ll often find them sprinkled throughout political addresses. They help to make the speaker’s point more clear, and they often resonate with the audience, prompting them to reflect further on an idea.

8f48aacc8181104e2625.text: Take this example, delivered by President Barack Obama in 2014:

687d140833b8e362f7ba.text: "Are we a nation that tolerates the hypocrisy of a system where

9ab97b80355d877666f3.text: workers who pick our fruit and make our beds never have a chance to get right with the law? Are we a nation that accepts the cruelty of ripping children from their parents' arms? Or are we a nation that values families, and works to keep them together?" By juxtaposing two very different scenarios through striking imagery, the

69623590454f195c5ec2.text: president was trying to remind the American people of their values and the policies he wanted (and didn’t want) them to support.

e0285c04b56a5a642cf5.text: Below are several examples of rhetorical questions from literature.

44a1adb1a2c910102d6c.text: The Merchant of Venice by William Shakespeare

bf8fb58d5deafa3c0ff0.text: "If you prick us, do we not bleed? If you tickle us, do we not laugh? If you poison us, do we not die?

4e2908bde687ebfdd911.text: And if you wrong us, shall we not revenge?"

efaa4202cbb7f7caa7e5.text: These questions, posed by the character of Shylock in The Merchant of

2768add4bad1ca62b900.text: Venice, don’t really need answers; the point is that the answer to each question above should be obvious. Romeo and Juliet by William Shakespeare

7cf6125f8ea95e20b760.text: "What’s in a name? That which we call a rose By any other name would smell as sweet.”

fcf1239454d005cadf35.text: Juliet’s question of “what’s in a name?” is intended to make a point about

cc12f1f2c17ebd6d690c.text: how little significance a name should hold.

46334c9818e442234fe1.text: "What happens to a dream deferred? Does it dry up like a raisin in the sun?

ce39319d2c45bcb69c88.text: Or fester like a sore- And then run?

5283a8e98946ecc1ea20.text: Does it stink like rotten meat? Or crust and sugar over- like a syrupy sweet?"

ddc5ac1690caf8c2ee56.text: The questions posed in this poem by Langston Hughes also don’t require

ad1763117a82c624e83c.text: responses. The speaker is simply pondering what happens to a “dream deferred,” using creative language and imagery to convey the possibilities.

916fff3c069414748d01.text: If overused, too many rhetorical questions might make you come off as too

f81e41888ce20a901fa8.text: But when used skilfully and in combination with other rhetorical devices,

4d48f3617d0f1efad603.text: such as ethos, pathos, and logos, rhetorical questions can enhance your speech and writing by emphasizing key points.

1e0df8117e5419053481.text: Rhetorical questions are not a necessity, but they can be valuable. They

d7a1cea1d102312a30f6.text: can be used in many different ways to: • Engage the audience • Increase the variety of your presentation • Influence and persuade the audience • Subtly draw attention and emphasize specific points • Introduce topics/ideas • Make the listeners think about certain topics

e4baaecfe3ad7c227f20.text: How to Use Rhetorical Questions in a Speech

478ced882c49201fafc7.text: Ask a rhetorical question to engage the audience and pause to allow them

d68227c3cfb26ab459ae.text: to think of an answer. This gets the audience to actively participate rather than passively listen as they create hypotheses or resolutions.

b4a6db6d634b2c80ace8.text: For example: asking "Why is practicing mindfulness beneficial for reducing

9c0d754619ae6ad5e4fd.text: anxiety?" would be more effective than saying "Practicing mindfulness exercises can reduce anxiety levels because..."

134b6958a66bbdb5bf77.text: Speakers may start presentations with rhetorical questions to increase the

5e9962f7c3b577594efd.text: likelihood of the audience staying engaged.

ad1b96cdad11d5c3bf09.text: Make the audience feel as though you are speaking to each member

19c70b8a65dda3548b77.text: For example: asking "Do you want to lose weight without feeling hungry?"

8a5e43c2796ce40b8c95.text: would be more effective than asking "Does anyone here want to lost weight without feeling hungry?" 3. Persuade The Audience

7f4748e0582c7e31e187.text: To get your audience to agree with you, ask a rhetorical question where the

47a979137509d0c578de.text: answer is clearly a "yes". Once the audience begins agreeing with you they are more likely to continue agreeing. You will be familiar with this type of persuasion in casual conversation, for example, "Nice weather today, isn't it?"

3e7d321b1fde8015d0ad.text: Another way to get the audience to agree with you is to show them that

ab34e70e2492a79571bd.text: you're similar. Show your listeners that you have shared experiences and that you understand their problems.

d0123cb9d06f2a17f019.text: For example, "We've all experienced being so stressed at work that we come

ff8422b8233332aad81d.text: home and don't feel like doing anything, haven't we?" 4. Evoke Emotions

7552828c2045c3fe9327.text: Make the audience feel the same way you do about something by asking

2cc203d259701226a565.text: For example, rather than saying "X has never helped our community" ask

d5dedc80fc043c6f32dc.text: "What has X ever done for our community?" This will trigger a strong emotional response because the audience will come to that conclusion that "X haven't done anything." 5. Emphasize a Statement

890f729dbd63597527da.text: After a statement has been made use a rhetorical question to get the

cb040e43a8122d0c3ed6.text: audience to think about that statement.

fbee4f48cd1cc4890053.text: For example, "The amount of plastic in the ocean is rising at a considerable

da33443f6d7571df0059.text: rate. How much damage will it take for you to help reduce this?"

ff8387c9a0e9f083674a.text: Think about your topic and audience when planning your speech. Try to

906717d6cb71187a1649.text: predict what the audience may want to ask. In your speech use the predictions as rhetorical questions and answer them.

3020baaf0a4f013faa75.text: For example, "As a dog owner you may think 'What should I be focusing on

7dc19e207301dfaaca40.text: to keep my dog healthy?' The answer is providing your dog with the correct nutrition and therefore food."

c3e84bf985bf64032359.text: You could also introduce one or more rhetorical questions at the start of

6ac74b1c99ac482f0a5f.text: your speech and explain that you will answer them during your speech. For example: "In the next 20 minutes let's explore the answers to these questions." Asking these difficult questions and promising you will provide the answers will increase interest and attention. 7. Answer Questions with Questions

98b57c2f1345b1965cea.text: Answer a question, either an audience member's or your own, using another

3d109da185c2a36c10ad.text: rhetorical question. Generally, both the questions have the same answer.

bac0658fefd483f7b41d.text: For example: "Have we met the targets again this year? Is the Pope

16f593c5b60ef6b6fc8f.text: Try to make the second question unique and relatable to the audience

f52951bde227fcc195af.text: because common examples can sound cheesy. 8. Consecutive Rhetorical Questions

4f62d82409965a27758e.text: • Increase the impact of your argument

2a5a899b04ba882a1a18.text: Ask multiple rhetorical questions consecutively - each one more specific or

4b9503cfccb90c393456.text: more powerful than the previous. This way your content will have a greater impact on the listeners.

b24aea3233a7a8cfa020.text: For example: "Isn't their skin lovely? Don't you think it looks really clear?

46fd3e4bf042e80a701a.text: Can you see any blemishes? Wouldn't you like to have skin like that?" • Show conflicting opinions

8221d23c8e56d67e475c.text: Use rhetorical questions consecutively to highlight the complexity of a topic

4f1d6edd569b052dabd2.text: by asking questions in which the answers provide conflicting viewpoints.

8d1b79db0e3d1db18364.text: For example: "How can we reduce the crime rate in the UK? Should we

b1beaf4f508e721ef627.text: rehabilitate offenders? Should criminals be punished with longer sentences? Should we create initiatives targeting at-risk children?"

9b4df9271d0c107e392d.text: If you start your speech with this technique, you can structure your speech

79743599fef2e5c07508.text: or presentation around it, with each section addressing a different viewpoint. • Show supporting opinions

1dd134242410454d0240.text: You can also consecutively ask questions in which the answers provide

3fa2bd67ee2a581f74ab.text: similar viewpoints. This is similar to repetition which is used to continually highlight an important point.

74f757564b0bf971e0cc.text: For example: "Which company achieves over 90% in customer satisfaction?

95f3da21eef7af2a5ced.text: Which company provides one of the best employee benefits programs in the

5b4545b7a95ad402a4cb.text: country? Which company scores highest in employee happiness and fulfilment? Of course, our company does!"

00448bef2e6acc3d83ae.text: Rhetorical questions are an effective way to gain the support of the audience

7dc24d5e33c786619718.text: but ensure that you do your research beforehand. This means finding out who your audience are, such as, their general views, attitudes, age etc. With this information you can plan rhetorical questions that will be appropriate and tailored to your listeners.
